dangerZoneNotes: Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours (1 hour if ambient temp exceeds 90F).
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
storageFreezer: Whole: up to 12 months at 0F; pieces: 9 months; ground: 3-4 months
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours. Ground meat has more surface area exposed to bacteria.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours. Rest time of 3 minutes after removing from heat source is critical for pasteurization.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours. Updated in 2011: pork no longer requires 160F. 145F with 3-min rest is safe.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Pre-cooked ham must reach 165F when reheating. Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
storageFridge: 3-5 days at 40F or below (opened); 2 weeks (unopened, vacuum-sealed)
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

item: Fish (fin fish: salmon, cod, halibut, etc.)
dangerZoneNotes: Fish is highly perishable. Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours. Cook until flesh is opaque and flakes easily.
coolingProtocol: Cool rapidly. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 1 hour.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath in sealed bag, change water every 30 min
storageFreezer: 3-8 months at 0F (fatty fish shorter, lean fish longer)
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Shellfish is extremely perishable. Cook until flesh is opaque. Shrimp: pink and firm. Lobster: red shell, opaque flesh. Scallops: milky white and firm.
coolingProtocol: Cool rapidly. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 1 hour.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath in sealed bag, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Discard any that do not open during cooking. Live shellfish should close when tapped; discard any that stay open before cooking.
coolingProtocol: Cool rapidly. Serve immediately or chill within 1 hour.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath in sealed bag
storageFridge: 1-2 days live at 40F (store in breathable container, not sealed plastic)
storageFreezer: 2-3 months at 0F (shucked); do not freeze live
sourceLabel: FDA Selecting and Serving Fresh and Frozen Seafood Safely

dangerZoneNotes: Parasites are the primary concern. FDA requires freezing to -4F (-20C) for 7 days, or -31F (-35C) for 15 hours to kill parasites before raw service. Tuna is often exempt.
coolingProtocol: Keep at 32F or below at all times. Never break the cold chain.
storageFridge: 1 day at 32F or below after thawing
sourceLabel: FDA Selecting and Serving Fresh and Frozen Seafood Safely

dangerZoneNotes: Cook eggs until yolk and white are firm for highest safety. For dishes served immediately, 145F is acceptable if consumed right away.
coolingProtocol: Refrigerate cooked egg dishes within 2 hours. Cool rapidly.
thawingMethods: Not applicable (do not freeze raw shell eggs)
storageFridge: 3-5 weeks in shell at 40F or below; 3-4 days hard-boiled
storageFreezer: Up to 12 months (beaten eggs only, not in shell)
sourceLabel: USDA Shell Eggs from Farm to Table

dangerZoneNotes: Custards and egg-based sauces are high risk. Do not hold between 40-140F for more than 2 hours.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
storageFreezer: 2-3 months (quiche, casserole); do not freeze custard
sourceLabel: USDA Shell Eggs from Farm to Table

dangerZoneNotes: All leftovers must be reheated to 165F regardless of original safe temp. Do not reheat more than once.
coolingProtocol: Refrigerate within 2 hours. Divide large quantities into shallow containers for faster cooling.
sourceLabel: USDA Leftovers and Food Safety

item: Stuffing and dressing (cooked inside or outside bird)
dangerZoneNotes: Stuffing inside a bird must reach 165F independently of the bird's temperature. Safer to cook stuffing outside the bird.
coolingProtocol: Remove stuffing from bird immediately after cooking. Cool separately.
sourceLabel: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart

dangerZoneNotes: Low-and-slow smoking passes through the danger zone slowly. Keep smoker above 225F to limit time in danger zone. Do not cold-smoke meats without a curing step.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours. Slice or pull meat before cooling for faster temperature drop.
thawingMethods: Cold water bath, change water every 30 min
sourceLabel: USDA Smoking Meat and Poultry

dangerZoneNotes: Dry-cured meats (salami, prosciutto) are shelf-stable until cut. Once sliced, refrigerate. Bacon must be cooked before serving; cook to desired crispness (no FDA minimum temp for commercially cured bacon, but 145F is recommended).
coolingProtocol: Refrigerate after opening or slicing.
storageFridge: Opened: 3-5 days (bacon), 2-3 weeks (dry cured whole); sliced deli: 3-5 days
storageFreezer: 1-2 months (bacon); dry-cured not recommended for freezing
sourceLabel: USDA Bacon and Food Safety

dangerZoneNotes: Pasteurized dairy products must be kept at 40F or below at all times. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Raw (unpasteurized) milk carries additional risk.
coolingProtocol: Return to refrigerator promptly after use.
thawingMethods: Not applicable (do not freeze milk for food safety, only for baking use)
storageFridge: 5-7 days after opening (milk); 1-2 weeks (heavy cream); check sell-by date
storageFreezer: 3 months (milk, for cooking only; texture changes)
sourceLabel: FDA Food Safety and Dairy Products

item: Soft cheeses (brie, camembert, ricotta, queso fresco)
dangerZoneNotes: Soft cheeses made with unpasteurized milk carry Listeria risk, especially for pregnant clients and immunocompromised individuals. Always verify pasteurization status.
coolingProtocol: Keep refrigerated. Bring to room temp for serving 30-60 minutes before, return leftovers promptly.
sourceLabel: FDA Food Safety and Dairy Products

item: Hard and aged cheeses (cheddar, parmesan, gruyere)
dangerZoneNotes: Lower risk than soft cheeses due to lower moisture content. Surface mold on hard cheese can be cut away (1 inch around and below mold). Do not do this with soft cheeses.
coolingProtocol: Keep refrigerated. Can sit at room temp for cheese boards for 2-4 hours safely.
sourceLabel: FDA Food Safety and Dairy Products

dangerZoneNotes: Salted butter can sit at room temperature for 1-2 days safely in a covered dish. Unsalted butter should be refrigerated at all times.
coolingProtocol: Return to refrigerator after use.
sourceLabel: FDA Food Safety and Dairy Products

dangerZoneNotes: Leafy greens are a leading cause of foodborne illness outbreaks (E. coli, Salmonella). Wash thoroughly under running water even if labeled 'pre-washed'. Do not soak.
coolingProtocol: Keep refrigerated at all times. Do not leave dressed salads at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
thawingMethods: Not applicable (do not freeze raw leafy greens for salad use)
storageFridge: 3-7 days at 40F (whole heads last longer than pre-cut)
storageFreezer: Not recommended for raw salad use
sourceLabel: FDA Selecting and Serving Produce Safely

dangerZoneNotes: Cooked potatoes and root vegetables are a TCS (time/temperature control for safety) food. Do not hold cooked roots between 40-140F for more than 2 hours. Raw roots at cool room temp are fine.
coolingProtocol: Once cooked, cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours.
thawingMethods: Not applicable (store raw at cool room temp or refrigerator)
storageFridge: Cooked: 3-5 days. Raw potatoes: do not refrigerate (starch converts to sugar). Raw carrots/beets: 2-4 weeks.
storageFreezer: Cooked: 2-3 months. Raw: blanch first, then freeze 8-12 months.
sourceLabel: FDA Selecting and Serving Produce Safely

dangerZoneNotes: Berries are fragile and can harbor pathogens. Wash gently under running water just before use; do not soak. Hepatitis A outbreaks have been linked to frozen berries.
coolingProtocol: Keep refrigerated. Do not wash until ready to use (moisture promotes mold).
thawingMethods: Room temperature (30-60 min for baking/cooking use)
sourceLabel: FDA Selecting and Serving Produce Safely

dangerZoneNotes: Cut melon is a TCS food. Bacteria on the rind transfers to flesh when cut. Wash rind thoroughly before cutting. Refrigerate cut melon within 2 hours (1 hour if above 90F).
coolingProtocol: Refrigerate cut melon immediately. Discard if left at room temperature more than 2 hours.
sourceLabel: FDA Selecting and Serving Produce Safely

dangerZoneNotes: Sprouts are high risk. Warm, humid growing conditions are ideal for bacteria. FDA advises cooking sprouts thoroughly for at-risk populations. Even 'thoroughly washed' sprouts can carry pathogens.
coolingProtocol: Keep refrigerated at all times.
sourceLabel: FDA Selecting and Serving Produce Safely

dangerZoneNotes: Cooked rice is a common source of Bacillus cereus. Spores survive cooking and multiply rapidly at room temperature. Never leave cooked rice at room temperature for more than 1 hour.
coolingProtocol: Cool rapidly by spreading in a thin layer. Refrigerate within 1 hour of cooking.
storageFridge: 1-2 days at 40F or below (shorter than most leftovers due to B. cereus risk)
sourceLabel: FDA Safe Food Handling

dangerZoneNotes: Tofu is a TCS food once opened. Keep refrigerated and submerged in water (change daily). Cook to 140F minimum for hot-hold service.
coolingProtocol: Refrigerate after opening. Change water daily for unused portions.
storageFridge: 3-5 days after opening (in water, changed daily); 2-3 months unopened (check date)
sourceLabel: FDA Safe Food Handling

dangerZoneNotes: Reheat to 165F (rolling boil recommended for soups and stocks). Large pots cool slowly; use ice bath or divide into shallow containers.
coolingProtocol: Cool from 135F to 70F within 2 hours, then from 70F to 40F within 4 more hours. Use ice bath or divide into shallow containers for large batches.
sourceLabel: USDA Leftovers and Food Safety

dangerZoneNotes: Sous vide pasteurization is time AND temperature dependent. At 150F, chicken breast (1 inch thick) requires 1 hour 11 minutes for full pasteurization. At 165F, pasteurization is instant.
coolingProtocol: Ice bath immediately after cooking if not serving right away. Cool to 40F within 1 hour.
sourceLabel: Douglas Baldwin, A Practical Guide to Sous Vide Cooking (pasteurization tables)

dangerZoneNotes: At 140F, pork tenderloin (1.5 inch diameter) requires 1 hour 50 minutes for pasteurization. Lower temps are possible but require longer times and carry more risk.
coolingProtocol: Ice bath immediately if not serving. Cool to 40F within 1 hour.
sourceLabel: Douglas Baldwin, A Practical Guide to Sous Vide Cooking (pasteurization tables)

dangerZoneNotes: At 130F, a 1-inch beef steak requires 1 hour 30 minutes for pasteurization. This yields medium-rare. Sear after sous vide for crust development.
coolingProtocol: Ice bath immediately if not searing right away. Cool to 40F within 1 hour.
sourceLabel: Douglas Baldwin, A Practical Guide to Sous Vide Cooking (pasteurization tables)

dangerZoneNotes: At 130F, a 1-inch salmon fillet requires 45 minutes for pasteurization. Yields a medium, silky texture. Higher temps give firmer, more opaque result.
coolingProtocol: Ice bath immediately if not serving. Cool to 40F within 1 hour.
sourceLabel: Douglas Baldwin, A Practical Guide to Sous Vide Cooking (pasteurization tables)

dangerZoneNotes: At 145F, eggs require 1 hour 15 minutes for a soft-set, custard-like texture. At 155F for 1 hour: firmer white, jammy yolk. At 165F for 1 hour: fully set.
coolingProtocol: Ice bath if not serving immediately.
sourceLabel: Douglas Baldwin, A Practical Guide to Sous Vide Cooking (pasteurization tables)
